data.title: Which Funds With Bank Exposure Best Capture The Data Leak Fallout?
data.description:
Funds tied to banks and financial services can look almost identical from their names. Pick one without checking what it actually owns and you can end up with a very different risk mix than you meant, especially around companies like Visa, Mastercard or JPMorgan. A fresh reminder just arrived, as hackers leaked customer data tied to those three through third party vendors. If banks manage to tighten vendor security without losing customers in the process, that could matter for how you compare three ETFs here: FTXO, EUFN and IYG, as different ways into the same story.

Where could strong businesses be hiding behind a cheap share price? Explore 35 high quality undervalued stocks combining solid balance sheets and cash flows with potential value beyond the headline.

First Trust Nasdaq Bank ETF (FTXO)

Holdings: 51 | In banks: 99.7% of the fund

Wells Fargo is the largest position at 8.08% and is a big diversified bank, with consumer and corporate clients that feel vendor data issues quickly through call volumes, fraud checks and product tweaks. U.S. Bancorp at 8.03% and JPMorgan at 7.88% add more large US lenders, and together the top two holdings are 16.1% of the fund. The ETF leans almost entirely on diversified and regional banks, so the data leak story feeds straight into how these businesses handle fraud monitoring, customer retention and the cost of tightening third party oversight.

Investors get a basket where no single stock dominates. Yet large players that handle payments, credit cards and corporate cash management still matter for how the story plays out. That structure leaves you depending on how well traditional banks as a group absorb higher compliance and vendor management costs into their day to day operations without major, long lasting customer shifts.

An ETF's price is just the sum of what it holds. Check whether FTXO trades above or below its holdings' estimated cash flow value.

iShares MSCI Europe Financials ETF (EUFN)

Holdings: 95 | In banks: 56.2% of the fund

This ETF gives you European banks at the front of the story, with a wide mix of financials around them. HSBC Holdings at 8.87% and Banco Santander at 5.04% are large lenders that feel higher vendor due-diligence and fraud monitoring costs directly when incidents touch card transactions or linked accounts. Allianz at 5.73% comes at the issue from the insurance side, where cyber risk cover and operational resilience services can see more attention when data leaks hit payments giants.

Investors are relying on a regional blend where 56.2% is in diversified banks and sizeable portions sit in insurance, capital markets and exchanges, so the leak-related burden does not fall on one type of business. That spread can dampen any single shock, although it also means the story is less focused than a banks heavy ETF. HSBC at 8.87% carries distinctly more of the fund than Santander at 5.04%.

iShares U.S. Financial Services ETF (IYG)

Holdings: 101 | In banks: 31.8% of the fund

Visa at 9.84% is the clearest link to the data leak, since its network sits close to where card fraud and chargebacks show up. Berkshire Hathaway at 14.98% and JPMorgan at 12.48% pull the story wider, because they bring insurance, banking and capital markets businesses that feel vendor security costs differently and can spread them across multiple lines. With 31.8% of IYG in diversified and regional banks and much of the rest in payment processors, brokers and exchanges, this ETF ties the banks theme to the broader US financial system rather than only to lenders.

Berkshire and JPMorgan together make up 27.5% of IYG, so investors rely heavily on how those two handle operational risk, regulatory responses and customer trust. The fund also leans on how payment and data heavy groups such as Visa secure their systems without losing transaction volume. This structure means most of the basket benefits if confidence in digital payments and large US financial institutions holds up, but investors still need to weigh that top heavy structure and the 0.37% fee against alternatives charging 0.49%.

What separates these funds

If you want the data leak story mostly through traditional lenders, FTXO and EUFN keep you closest to the sector. FTXO is almost entirely in banks, spread between diversified and regional lenders, and its largest position is smaller than IYG’s, so you are less tied to a single company response. EUFN blends big European banks like HSBC and Banco Santander with insurance and capital markets groups, which dilutes any one vendor incident but keeps more than half the portfolio in lenders that still face fraud, remediation and compliance work.

IYG takes a different angle. Only about a third of the fund is in banks and much more sits in payment processors, brokers and exchanges, so Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan pull more of the story. If banks and payments firms shore up vendor security without large fines or lasting customer loss, that mix may be attractive to some investors. Your choice depends on your preferred type of exposure and which blend of holdings, concentration, history and fee structure aligns with your own objectives.
